title: Welcome to STR Concierge: What's Different About Owning
section: Part Two · Module 0 - Ownership vs. Arbitrage

slides.kicker: Part Two · Module 0 · Ownership vs. Arbitrage
slides.title: Owning swaps a lease's capped risk for an open-ended one, so check every deal at ten gates
slides.subtitle: Lesson 0.1. Welcome to STR Concierge: What's Different About Owning
meta: Cedar Ridge house, with Alder Street for contrast (hypothetical)
Education only. Not legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
Welcome to Part Two. This is STR Concierge, the ownership side of the course. STR means short-term rental.

In Part One you learned to lease a unit and run it. Here you buy the house. That sounds like the same business with a bigger check. It isn't quite. The check is bigger, the loan runs for decades, and you'll hear from more professionals before you commit.

So this first lesson is a map. I'm not teaching any single step in depth today. Each later lesson does that. By the end of this one, you should be able to say who holds title and who carries the loan. You'll also know who pays for a new roof, and who makes the final call. You'll see the course as ten go/no-go gates. And you'll know which gates can end a deal, and roughly how much money is on the line when you reach each one.

I'll use Cedar Ridge, the lake house Maya and Chris are looking at. I'll hold it next to Alder Street, the Part One apartment, so you can see the difference in real numbers.

slides.title: A lease has edges; owning removes them
slides.text: A lease has edges. Owning removes them: you buy the building, the land under it, and every problem inside the walls.
slides.support: Pricing, cleaning, guest messages, and local rules still apply. What's new is the size of the commitment and the number of professionals you need to hear from.
slides.notes:
Think about what capped your downside at Alder Street. The lease had a term. The furniture had a price. The rent was a known monthly number. If things went badly, you knew roughly where the bottom was.

Owning takes those edges away. You buy the building and the land under it. You sign a loan that runs for decades. Your cash goes in as a down payment and closing costs, and it doesn't come back out unless you refinance or sell.

That's the whole reason STR Concierge is its own program. Your Part One skills still work here. Pricing, cleaning, guest communication, and local rules all carry over. What changes is how much you commit, and how many professionals you need before you commit it.

Keep that frame for the rest of Module 0. Every table I show you is really asking two things. How big is the commitment? And who do you need to hear from before you make it? You still make the call.

slides.title: As an owner you hold title, carry the loan, and pay for the roof
rows: Landlord owns it. You hold a lease.
You, or your entity, hold title
A mortgage on the house; the lender may want a personal guarantee
Deposit, first month, furniture, setup, reserve
Down payment, closing costs, furniture, repairs, reserves
Principal and interest, property tax, insurance, any HOA
Usually the landlord's for structure and systems
Capital repairs (roof, HVAC, septic, water heater)
Usually the landlord's, per the lease
Yours, in large amounts at irregular times
slides.notes:
Here's the side-by-side. I want you to read two rows twice: maintenance and capital repairs. Maintenance is routine upkeep. Capital repairs replace a big piece of the building.

At Alder Street, if the water heater fails, it's usually the landlord's problem. You lose a few nights, you call them, and they fix it. Check your lease, but that's the normal split.

At Cedar Ridge, it's your bill and your emergency. You pick the plumber. You approve the cost. You pay it that same week. Roofs, HVAC, septic, and water heaters don't break on a schedule. They come in big amounts at odd times.

The loan row matters too. A mortgage is secured by the house. Depending on the loan, the lender may also want a personal guarantee. That means your household can be on the hook, and not just the property.

And look at up-front cash. The operator's list is deposit, first month, and furniture. The owner's list starts with a down payment and closing costs, and it still needs furniture and reserves on top.

slides.title: Owning the deed does not give you the right to host; only local rules do
rows: The city, plus the landlord's written permission
The city and any HOA. No landlord to ask.
Your STR liability policy; landlord insures the building
You insure the building and liability; the lender requires coverage
The landlord can refuse, end, or not renew
You decide, and you carry the result
Lease ends, or you negotiate an early exit
Sell, refinance, change use, or hold. Each costs time and money.
Cash flow and an operating skill
Cash flow, loan paydown, possible value change, possible tax timing (depreciation can shift when you owe tax)

box.label: Before you host
box.text: Airbnb tells hosts to check HOA or co-op rules and local laws first ([Airbnb Help, article 1397](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1397)).

slides.notes:
The approvals row changes shape when you own. In arbitrage, a landlord can say no, and many do. As an owner, there's no landlord gate. That feels like freedom. But the city, the county, and any homeowners association still apply.

Airbnb's own help center tells hosts to check HOA or co-op rules and local laws before hosting. Owning the deed doesn't give you the right to run a short-term rental at that address. Only the local rules do. We'll turn that into a hard gate in a minute.

Now the last row. An owner can earn from four places at once: cash flow, loan paydown, a change in value, and tax timing. Tax timing means depreciation can lower your tax now, and some of it can come back when you sell. An operator earns mainly from one. Four streams sound better, and sometimes they are. But each one carries its own cost. Some of them never reach your bank account until you sell.

That's exactly what lesson 0.2 tests with numbers. For now, just notice that "what you build" is a longer list with longer strings attached.

slides.notes:
This is the whole program on one slide. It runs in one direction. You start with "what should I buy" and you end with "is it performing the way I underwrote it". Underwriting is just your spreadsheet estimate of what the property will earn and cost.

The codes are simple. The 0.x lessons are this readiness module. PA lessons cover buying the property. OP lessons cover operating it.

My lessons teach the decisions. Sam's lessons are the live demos. So after PA.1, Sam takes you through market choice, deal sourcing, underwriting, and a tax demo in PA.2 to PA.5. Then I pick up with financing in PA.6.

Look at where readiness sits. It comes before the buy box, and the buy box comes before any market research. That order is on purpose. The cash stack is every dollar you need on day one, plus reserves. If you can't fund it, the best market in the country doesn't help you.

Don't try to memorize this table. Come back to it when you're lost in the middle of the program and want to know where you are.
slides.text: 0.x = readiness, PA = buying, OP = operating. I teach the decisions; Sam runs the live demos.

slides.title: Each stage hands the next one a document, so a skipped stage leaves a gap

nodes.d: What you'll buy and when you pass

slides.text: If you skip a stage, the next one has nothing reliable to work from. PA.5 to PA.7 add a tax demo and the loan; this chain is the document trail.
slides.notes:
Here's why the order matters. Each stage produces a document, and the next stage uses it.

PA.1 produces your buy box. Sam's PA.2 and PA.3 use that buy box to pick a market and build a list of properties. PA.4 produces an underwriting package for one property. PA.8 uses that package to set your offer ceiling. Then PA.9 checks the package against what the inspector and the city actually say. PA.5 to PA.7 sit in between. They add a tax demo and the loan, but they don't change this chain.

So picture someone who skips the buy box and goes straight to touring houses. What does Sam's pipeline filter on? Nothing. What does the underwriting test against? Their mood that day.

Or picture someone who skips underwriting and makes an offer. There's no ceiling. The offer price is whatever feels right in the moment, and the diligence check has no numbers to compare against.

That's what I mean by a gap. Each document is the input to the next decision. When you're tempted to jump ahead, ask which document you're missing.

slides.title: Each professional answers inside one lane, and you combine the answers
rows: Comparable sales, offer terms, contingency timing, local practice
Whether STR use is legal at the address; your tax result
Whether you qualify, rate and points, reserves, what income counts
Whether the deal is a good investment for you
The physical condition of the house and its systems
Condition problems an inspection would find
Whether they'll write an STR policy, the cost, the exclusions
Whether platform protection replaces a policy (don't assume it does)
slides.notes:
Owning brings more people into the deal. Each one has a narrow job. Trouble starts when you ask someone a question that belongs to someone else.

Your agent knows comparable sales and offer terms. Your agent does not know whether short-term rental use is legal at that address, and shouldn't be guessing about your taxes.

Your lender tells you whether you qualify, the rate and points, and what income they'll count. Points are upfront loan fees. The lender does not tell you whether this is a good investment. A lender approval means they expect to be repaid. It says nothing about whether you'll be happy.

The inspector and the appraiser get mixed up all the time. The inspector looks at condition. The appraiser estimates value for the lender. Neither does the other's job.

And the insurance agent tells you whether they'll write a short-term rental policy on this specific house. Don't assume platform protection replaces that policy. We'll come back to that in PA.12.

You make the final call on every gate. These people each hand you one fact.

slides.title: Title, tax, and local help each answer a narrow question, never your whole deal
rows: Who owns it now, liens, easements, how money moves at closing
Depreciation, losses, personal use, and sale tax for your household
Whether the lender will approve you
Contract terms, HOA documents, entity and title, local STR law
Turnovers, access, repairs, guest issues on the ground
Legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice
slides.notes:
Here's the rest of the team.

Title and escrow tell you who owns the property now, what liens and easements sit on it, and how money moves at closing. They don't tell you whether the city allows short-term rentals there. A clean title says nothing about zoning.

Your CPA handles depreciation, losses, personal-use days, and tax on a future sale, for your household. Your CPA can't tell you whether a lender will approve you.

Bring in a real estate attorney as needed. Contract terms, HOA documents, entity and title questions, and local short-term rental law are their lane.

Your local cleaner, handyman, and maybe a co-host run the ground game. Turnovers, access, repairs, guest problems. They don't set pricing strategy or make compliance calls.

And the STR Concierge team helps with the course process and the worksheets. We don't give legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice. Ask the team what support your membership includes.

slides.title: Other people do parts of the work, but you carry the result
items: The appraiser works for the lender. The inspector works for you, and hiring one is your job ([CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/close/schedule-a-home-inspection/)).
A lender's title policy protects the lender. An owner's policy protects your equity ([CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-owners-title-insurance-en-164/)).
On Airbnb, you set each co-host's permissions. You stay responsible for co-hosts, even ones a full-access co-host adds ([article 1534](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/1534)).
Each professional gives you a fact or an opinion inside their lane. You make the final decision at every gate.
slides.notes:
Three places where responsibility splits in a way new owners miss.

First, inspection. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is direct about this. The appraiser works for the lender's question, which is value. You, the buyer, are responsible for hiring the inspector. If you skip it, nobody else is checking the roof on your behalf.

Second, title insurance. The lender will require a lender's policy. That one protects the lender. If you want your own equity protected, that's an owner's policy. Ask about it at closing. PA.11 covers this.

Third, co-hosts. If you add a co-host on Airbnb later, you choose their permission level. But Airbnb says the listing owner remains responsible for co-hosts. That includes ones added by a full-access co-host. You can hand off tasks. You can't hand off accountability. OP.7 goes deeper on this.

The pattern across all three is the same. Other people do parts of the work. You carry the result.

slides.title: Gates 0 to 3 cost only time, so most bad deals should die here
rows: Can we fund the full cash stack and keep our emergency savings?
Wait, build cash, or lease (Part One)
Does it meet every hard requirement (must-have) in the buy box?
Is unhosted STR use (you don't live there) allowed at this exact address, including HOA rules?
Pass, or get it in writing first
Is the weak case inside our downside rule, using a lender's current rate and terms?
Pass, or plan a lower offer (PA.8)
Do we have a written quote we qualify for, with reserves we can meet?
slides.notes:
A deal moves forward only when it clears a gate. At each gate, one answer ends it. There are ten gates, numbered 0 to 9, and this slide shows the first five.

Gate 0 is readiness, from lesson 0.3. Gate 1 is your buy box. Gate 2 is permission at the exact address. Unhosted means you don't live there during the stay. SR.1 is the regulatory compliance checklist. Gate 3 is underwriting. The weak case is a bad-year version of your numbers. Your downside rule, from PA.1, is the most you'll accept losing in that year. Use a lender's current rate here. The written quote comes at Gate 4.

Gates 0 to 3 cost only time. Gate 2 and Gate 3 are where most bad deals should die. The city's rules are public. Sam's PA.4 underwriting runs in your own spreadsheet.

Here's the trap. A buyer who treats these gates as formalities tends to find the problem later, at Gate 6. By then the inspections are paid for and earnest money is on the line.

So when a house fails Gate 2, don't argue with it. Pass, or get a written answer before you spend another dollar.

slides.title: From Gate 5 on, real money is at stake, and Gate 6 runs on a contract clock
rows: Will the seller accept a price at or below our walk-away number?
Do inspection, insurance, title, appraisal, and permit hold up, inside the contingency window?
Do the Closing Disclosure and wire instructions match what we agreed?
Stop and verify before money moves
Insured, safe, permitted, furnished, team in place?
Are actual results inside the range we underwrote?
slides.notes:
Here are the second five gates. Notice the money changes here.

Gate 5 is the offer. If the seller won't come to your walk-away number, you walk. PA.8 shows you how to set that number.

Gate 6 is diligence: inspection, insurance quote, title, appraisal, and permit. A No means a finding broke the numbers or the plan. Then you renegotiate or cancel. And this gate has a clock. Contingencies are conditions in your purchase contract that let you cancel, and they run on deadlines. Miss one, and your options can shrink, depending on the contract. PA.8 and PA.9 cover how to set those windows.

Gate 7 is closing. The Closing Disclosure is the lender's final statement of costs. Check it and the wire instructions against what you agreed. If anything is off, stop before money moves.

Gate 8 is launch. Don't publish the listing until it's insured, safe, permitted, furnished, and staffed.

Gate 9 happens after you own. It's the first time your underwriting meets reality. Sam walks through that review in OP.10.

slides.eyebrow: Worked example · Cash on day one
slides.title: Cedar Ridge needs $142,688 on day one, 7 times Alder Street's $20,370
slides.side:
The loan is $385,000 - $96,250 = $288,750. Cash to close on the DSCR quote is $96,250 + $11,550 + $2,888 = **$110,688**. DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) is the loan type quoted here; PA.6 explains it.

Alder Street needed **$20,370**: $12,050 of setup plus $8,320 of deposit, first month, and reserve.

$142,688 / $20,370 = **7.0**.

side_box.label: Still missing
side_box.text: No lender reserves or personal emergency savings yet. Lesson 0.3 adds them.

slides.notes:
Let's make it concrete. Maya and Chris are modeling a $385,000 price on Cedar Ridge, against a $399,000 asking price. That's the price the seller later accepts in PA.8. All of these figures are assumptions from the course's worked examples.

Step by step. The down payment is 25% of $385,000, which is $96,250. The loan is the rest, $288,750. Closing costs are 3% of price, $11,550. Their quote is a DSCR loan, short for debt service coverage ratio. It carries one point, and a point is a fee of 1% of the loan. That's another $2,888. So closing costs total $14,438, and cash to close is $110,688.

Then furnishing. The budget is $32,000. That brings cash in to $142,688.

Now hold that next to Alder Street. The apartment needed $20,370 on day one. That was $12,050 of sunk setup, plus $8,320 tied up in the deposit, first month, and an operating reserve.

$142,688 divided by $20,370 is 7.0. Seven times the cash. And the Cedar Ridge number still doesn't include lender reserves or the family's own emergency fund. Lesson 0.3 adds both.

slides.title: In a bad year Alder Street still nets $1,548, while Cedar Ridge loses $5,475
rows: Bad year (each property's own downside case)
Remaining rent (up to $46,800) minus what the unit still earns; per early-exit terms
A sale: $31,242 of costs (7% of an assumed $446,321 after 3% yearly growth); more if value falls
slides.text: PITIA means principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and association dues. The bad-year loss comes from reserves or from the household.
slides.notes:
Here's the rest of the comparison.

Monthly fixed cost first. Alder Street's rent is $1,950. Cedar Ridge's PITIA on the DSCR quote is $2,557. That's principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and association dues. There's no HOA, so the dues are zero. On top of that, the owner sets aside 5% of gross booking revenue for repairs and 5% for capital items. In the base case, gross is $74,275, so that's $7,428 a year.

Now the bad year. Each property has its own downside case. Alder Street's stress case still nets $1,548. Cedar Ridge's weak case loses $5,475 after debt service, and that already includes the set-asides. The money comes out of reserves or the household.

The way out is different too. At Alder Street, the worst case is the rest of the lease, up to $46,800, less what the unit still earns. At Cedar Ridge, it's a sale. The five-year example assumes 3% yearly growth, and selling costs are $31,242 before tax. If the value falls, the hit is bigger. So don't compare those two numbers directly.

Cedar Ridge offers back $2,795 of loan paydown in year one, possible value change, and possible tax timing. Lesson 0.2 tests all of it.

slides.title: Failing Gates 0 to 3 costs only time; by closing, $110,688 is committed
slides.caption: Running totals. Earnest money is 2% of price, as in PA.8 (assumption); refunds depend on the contract. Gate 6 adds about $1,500 of inspections (assumption), kept outside the $110,688 and $142,688 totals. The earnest money counts toward cash to close.
slides.notes:
Here's why early gates matter, in dollars. The bars are running totals of what Maya and Chris would have spent or committed by the time each gate is decided.

Gates 0 to 3 cost only time, and maybe a data subscription. Gate 4 might cost an application or credit report fee, depending on the lender.

At Gate 5, once the offer is accepted, earnest money goes in. I've used 2% of price, $7,700, the figure they agree in PA.8. Whether you get it back depends on your contract and its contingencies. At Gate 6, add about $1,500 of inspection fees for general, septic, and other specialist checks.

Then the jump. If Gate 7 fails, you stop and verify, so the $110,688 isn't lost. But if you close, that cash is committed. The earnest money counts toward it. It's also the number a wire-fraud scam targets. Gate 8 adds $32,000 of furnishing, plus carrying costs. Gate 9 comes after you own.

So Gates 0 to 3 cost only time. From Gate 5 on, it's thousands, then tens of thousands.

slides.title: For every serious property, log each gate, and leave it blank until it's in writing
rows: City or county; attorney if unclear
slides.notes:
This is your working tool for the whole buying phase. You don't have a property yet, so today you set up the blank log. Fill in Gate 0 after lesson 0.3. Then start a new copy for each property you seriously consider from the list you build in Sam's PA.3.

Fill in one row per gate as you reach it. The evidence column is the important one. It's a document, a link, or an email. "The agent said it's fine" is not evidence. "City code section and the date I read it" is.

Leave a gate blank until you have a written answer. An open gate is honest. A gate marked pass on a hunch leads people to Gate 6 with a problem they could have found at Gate 2.

When a property fails, write down what ended it. After a few logs, you'll see patterns. Maybe every lake house in your range fails insurance. Maybe every one with an HOA fails permission. That tells you something about your buy box and your market.

The log also makes the calls with your agent and lender faster. You're asking specific questions with the evidence in front of you.

slides.title: Five confirmations, each due before a set point in the deal
rows: STR use is allowed at the exact address and under HOA rules; STR attorney if unclear
Reserves, credit, down payment, and guarantees, in writing
Before you rely on the quote
They'll write an STR policy on this house, and what it excludes
How earnest money, inspection, and financing contingencies work, every deadline
How ownership, depreciation, and personal use affect your household's taxes
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what, and when.

The city or county licensing office confirms that short-term rental use is allowed at the exact address, and under any HOA rules. Do that before an offer. If the answer is unclear, get an STR attorney.

Your lender confirms reserves, credit, down payment, and any guarantee, in writing. A verbal "you should be fine" doesn't count.

Your insurance agent confirms they'll write a short-term rental policy on this specific house, and what it excludes. Get that before your diligence window closes. If you can't get it insured at a price the numbers can carry, treat that as a failed gate.

Your agent or attorney explains how earnest money and the inspection and financing contingencies work in your contract. That includes every deadline. Put those dates on a calendar the day you sign.

And your CPA confirms how ownership, depreciation, and personal use affect your household's taxes. Do that before you count any tax benefit in a decision. Until then, the tax benefit is zero in your math.

slides.title: Four short tasks set up your gate log and team this week
items: Copy the gate log into a sheet or notebook you'll keep open during the search. Fill in Gate 0 after lesson 0.3.
Write one paragraph: which gate you expect to be hardest for you, and why.
Using the team table, list the roles you don't have a name for yet. Next to each, write how you'll find one before PA.4.
Mark on your calendar that no offer goes out until Gates 0 to 4 have written evidence.
slides.next: Next: **0.2, Why Ownership Wins: Cash Flow + Tax Savings + Equity.** It tests the four possible streams on Cedar Ridge, one case where owning works and one where it doesn't.
slides.notes:
Four things before the next lesson. None of them should take more than an hour.

First, set up the gate log somewhere you'll really use it. A spreadsheet, a notebook, whatever you'll keep open. You'll fill in Gate 0 after lesson 0.3.

Second, answer the first exercise question in writing. Which gate do you expect to be hardest for you, and why? Be honest. For some people it's readiness. For others it's walking away at Gate 5 when they love the house.

Third, answer the second question. Look at the team table. Who don't you have a name for yet? Write down how you'll find one before you reach PA.4. Two roles to find early are a lender and an insurance agent who writes short-term rental policies. You'll need a lender's numbers by PA.4.

Fourth, put a rule on your calendar: no offer until Gates 0 to 4 have written evidence.

Then go to lesson 0.2. You'll separate the money you can spend from the money locked in the house. And you'll see one case where owning Cedar Ridge works and one where it doesn't.

slides.text: Cedar Ridge and Alder Street figures come from the course's worked examples and are all assumptions. Inspection fees ($1,500) are a new assumption; the 2% earnest money matches PA.8.
slides.notes:
Here are the sources behind this lesson.

The two Airbnb help articles back the points about checking HOA and local rules before hosting, and about staying responsible for your co-hosts. The CFPB pages back the inspector versus appraiser split, and the difference between a lender's and an owner's title policy.

The STR Concierge Program Outline V1 is internal background. You don't need to read it, and it adds no lessons to the course path.

Every Cedar Ridge and Alder Street number in this deck comes from the course's worked examples. They are assumptions for teaching, not a real deal. The money-at-risk slide adds two assumptions: 2% earnest money, which matches PA.8, and about $1,500 of inspection fees.

Rules change. When you're looking at a real address, go back to the official page and check the date. Don't rely on my slide, or anyone's slide, for a rule that decides whether you can host.
